newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican welcomes Yeltsin's stand on religion bill.
newsitem.headline: Vatican welcomes Yeltsin's stand on religion bill.

text.p: The Vatican on Wednesday welcomed a decision by Russian President Boris Yeltsin to reject a controversial bill on religious freedom and said it hoped a new text could foster better relations with the Roman Catholic Church.

The Vatican said in a statement it noted with satisfaction Yeltsin's veto, which came after Pope John Paul wrote to him to warn that the survival of Catholicism in Russia could be threatened t if the bill became law.

"It is to be hoped that a new text can contribute to a better and more serene understanding of the religious reality in that great nation, where the Catholic Church has been present for centuries," the statement said.

Yeltsin said on Tuesday he had decided not to sign the draft law "On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Association" because it contradicted Russia's constitution guaranteeing equality for all confessions and would have led to religious conflicts.
The bill, overwhelmingly approved by both the Duma and the upper house, the Federation Council, and strongly supported by the powerful Russian Orthodox Church, favoured traditional faiths in Russia.
Apart from Orthodoxy, which Russians closely associate with their culture and national identity, these include Islam, Buddhism and Judaism.
It said only confessions that were registered at least 15 years ago -- when religion was still tightly controlled by the atheistic Communist Party -- could qualify as "religious organisations".
Others would have had to wait 15 years before applying for full legal rights. The bill would also have imposed new restrictions on foreign missionaries operating in Russia.
The U.S. Senate had threatened to withhold aid worth about $200 million if it had been approved.
The bill now goes back to parliament, in summer recess until September, for reconsideration. Yeltsin's veto could be overturned by a two-thirds majority in both chambers.
